narrative: The model estimated a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it is high enough that the admissions decision treated your application as too risky to approve. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: your first-decile position was far from the accepted-student average around the sixth decile, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score was the next most influential factor. At 36 it was slightly below the accepted average of about 37, but in your overall profile it worked as a modest counterweight toward passing rather than toward failure. Your middle family-income bracket was the third most influential factor and added a smaller push toward failure, even though about 35% of accepted students came from that bracket. The denial therefore reflects the combination of a first-decile third-year standing, a slightly below-average LSAT, and a smaller income-bracket effect; it was not based on your gender or race. Next, ask admissions whether human review is available and what evidence could offset the bar-risk estimate. Consider retaking the LSAT if feasible, completing bar-readiness or advanced law coursework, and documenting any upward trend or mitigating circumstances. A 77% estimate is not a bar to future success, but the application should directly address the academic risk factors.
